etymologies.etymologyHTML: First appears c. 1655, in the writings of Álvaro Semedo. From Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê) (Amoy dialect), from Old Chinese, ultimately from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la (“leaf, tea”). Introduced to English and other Western European languages by the Dutch East India Company, who sourced their tea in Amoy; compare Malay teh along the same trade route. Doublet of chai and cha (and, distantly, the first element of lahpet), from same Proto-Sino-Tibetan root; see discussion of cognates.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The tea plant (Camellia sinensis); (countable) a variety of this plant.
(uncountable) The dried leaves or buds of the tea plant; (countable) a variety of such leaves.
(uncountable) The drink made by infusing these dried leaves or buds in hot water.

quote.text: Mother […] considered that the exclusiveness of Peter's circle was due not to its distinction, but to the fact that it was an inner Babylon of prodigality and whoredom, from which every Kensingtonian held aloof, except on the conventional tip-and-run excursions in pursuit of shopping, tea and theatres.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Any similar drink made by infusing parts of various other plants.

quote.text: Tea was a very special institution, revolving as it did around the ceremony and worship of Toast. Toast, for reasons lost in time, was the substance chosen.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Semantic loan from Chinese 茶 (chá, “tea”).

definitions.definition: A moment, a historical unit of time from China, about the amount of time needed to quickly drink a traditional cup of tea. It is now found in Chinese-language historical fiction.
